newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire considers response to Ugandan attacks.
newsitem.headline: Zaire considers response to Ugandan attacks.

text.p: Zaire's authorities grappling with a Rwandan-backed rebellion in eastern Zaire are weighing how best to respond to attacks by Uganda, a military source said on Monday.
The source said the army leadership in consultation with political authorities were planning a full public statement on the next line of action.

The government accused Uganda of using tanks and armoured vehicles to capture the towns of Beni and Kasindi, just over 200 km (120 miles) from Goma, one of three key eastern towns seized by ethnic Tutsi rebels.
But missionary sources said on Monday Beni had been captured by Zairean rebels. They said local residents reported looting and raping by Zaire's ragged army as it fled further north.
A weekend Zaire statement accused Uganda of aggression.

"The occupation by Ugandan troops of the towns of Beni, coupled with declarations Uganda's government spokesman, who says the Ugandan soldiers will remain in Zaire until the Zairean governement stops aiding Uganda Moslem rebels...constitutes a pretext to justify unprovoked aggression against Zaire," Interior Minister Kamanda wa Kamanda said in the statement.

"Beni fell on Saturday," one of the missionary sources told Reuters in Nairobi, quoting missionaries evacuated from eastern Zaire. "Rebels moved swiftly to capture Beni after taking the town of Butembo."
Beni, so far the northernmost town lost by the Zaire army, is close to where the Ugandan troops have been attacking Ugandan rebels based on the Zairean side of the border.

Zaire denies aiding Ugandan rebels who have led attacks on positions on Ugandan territory from within Zaire over the past three weeks. The governement says the "hot-pursuit" of the rebels on Zairean soil is a pretext to aid Rwanda-backed rebels and other allies.

The government has repeatedly accused Uganda of involvement in the conflict in the east of the country, saying that its neighbour has supported operations by the regular armies of Rwanda and Burundi on Zairean soil.
In October and November Rwanda-baacked rebels captured a strip of teritory in the eastern Kivu provinces, routing the poorly equipped, ill-disciplined Zairean troops stationed there.
Since last week the Zairean rebels have been advancing north, taking the town of Butembo, and now heading towards the province of Haut-Zaire bordering Uganda and Sudan.

Diplomats in Kinshasa fear that the direct involvement of Ugandan troops considerably increases the difficulties in deploying an international force in the region and of finding a solution to the spreading conflict in eastern Zaire.
"The direct Ugandan involvement makes the situation that much more complicated to resolve," one senior Western diplomat told Reuters.
Following the weekend's events, Kamanda sent a statement to the Security Council, saying Uganda's involvement in the conflict disqualified the country as a base for U.N. troops.

Lieutenant-General Maurice Baril, the Canadian commander of the proposed multinational force to help feed Rwandan refugees and Zaireans displaced by the fighting in eastern Zaire, has set up a forward headquarters in Uganda's capital Kampala.
